video_title: Annie Lowrey on the Time Tax, Fraud, and Rationing by Paperwork
gist: Atlantic staff writer Annie Lowrey argues with Tyler Cowen that US government programs ration benefits by paperwork rather than by price or rules, costing roughly 50 hours per person per year, with the burden falling hardest on poor people, immigrants and people entangled with the criminal justice system. Cowen repeatedly presses the contrarian case that administrative friction is a useful rationing and screening device — for Medicare procedures, disability, immigration and even voting — while Lowrey counters that fraud is overwhelmingly provider-side, that improper payments are a function of rule complexity, and that simpler federal administration plus AI agents would cut both burden and fraud. She also concedes her earlier pro-UBI book was too optimistic about ancillary benefits, while arguing AI-driven white-collar disruption revives the UBI case.

insights.claim: Annie Lowrey estimates the aggregate bureaucratic time burden in the US at roughly 50 hours per person per year — about an hour a week — drawing on the American Time Use Survey.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: A ~50-hour national time levy is a quantifiable drag on labor supply and household throughput, and it sizes the addressable market for AI form-filling and compliance-automation tools.
insights.quote: it’s 50 hours per person per year

insights.claim: Lowrey believes the 50-hour figure is an undercount because the American Time Use Survey cannot capture multitasking — waiting on hold while cooking dinner registers only as cooking — and because bureaucratic time is scattered across many categories that are never agglomerated.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: If the true burden is materially higher than official time-use data implies, the policy return on administrative simplification is systematically understated in cost-benefit analysis.
insights.quote: Again, I don’t think that ATUS is picking up a lot of data.

insights.claim: OIRA, the federal office nominally responsible for paperwork burden, does not functionally measure the time cost of administrative burden at all, according to Lowrey.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: There is no authoritative federal scorekeeper for administrative burden, so reform pressure has to originate outside government — a gap that outside data and journalism can fill.
insights.quote: The other issue is that OIRA does not measure this functionally at all.

insights.claim: The groups paying the highest time taxes are people involved with the criminal justice system, immigrants, and poor people, making administrative burden a sharply regressive levy.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Incidence means benefit take-up rates, not statutory generosity, are the real variable when forecasting safety-net outlays and low-income consumption.
insights.quote: People with involvement with the criminal justice system, immigrants, and poor people.

insights.claim: Wealthy people largely escape the time tax through subordination — paying accountants and staff to absorb it — but housing permitting is an exception where even very wealthy San Franciscans wait 500 days and sit through multiple rounds of public comment.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Permitting delay is the one administrative burden affluent constituents feel directly, which makes it the most politically tractable reform target — relevant to homebuilders in supply-constrained metros.
insights.quote: Even very, very wealthy people in San Francisco will wait 500 days for a permit, going through many rounds of public comment.

insights.claim: Lowrey frames time as the uniquely unexpandable tax base: government can tax work, income or natural resources because more of each can be produced, but it cannot create more of a citizen's time.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Treating time as a non-replenishable base reframes paperwork as a deadweight tax with no revenue offset — a reusable lens for scoring any regulatory or compliance proposal.
insights.quote: You could tax things that you can produce more of. More work, more income, more natural resources. You can’t give people more time.

insights.claim: Lowrey names TANF the single worst US program: roughly $16.5 billion a year that does not change the child poverty rate while being enormously onerous and punitive to comply with.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: A $16.5bn program with no measurable effect on its stated goal is the prime candidate for consolidation or conversion to cash in any future welfare reform cycle.
insights.quote: It’s a terrible waste of the $16.5 billion a year associated with it.

insights.claim: Lowrey's general rule is that US programs used mostly by higher-income Americans are administered far better than safety-net programs, with welfare the worst of all.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Administrative quality tracks the political power of the user base — a simple predictor of which programs attract digital investment and which stay broken.
insights.quote: Programs that are mostly used by higher-income Americans are much, much, much better.

insights.claim: Lowrey cites Social Security's retirement program and the postal service as the parts of US government that work well, noting the retirement program runs at less than 1 percent overhead and does all the work for the beneficiary.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Sub-1% overhead is the benchmark any privatized or means-tested alternative must beat, and the strongest empirical argument for universal, automatic benefit design.
insights.quote: it’s less than 1 percent overhead

insights.claim: In most peer democracies salaried workers do not file their own taxes — Japan requires nothing of salaried earners and other countries pre-fill returns — while the US IRS is legally barred from doing this even though nine in ten American households take the standard deduction.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: A legal prohibition, not technical difficulty, protects the US tax-prep industry's revenue base, making statutory change the single event risk for that sector.
insights.quote: The IRS is legally not allowed to do it.

insights.claim: Submerged, tax-code-delivered benefits such as the child tax credit achieve higher take-up because almost everyone files a return, but recipients frequently do not know they are receiving a benefit, which starves the program of the political constituency needed to defend it.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Delivery mechanism determines political durability: tax-code benefits are efficient but expire quietly, so CTC-style expansions are weak foundations for long-horizon consumption forecasts.
insights.quote: People had no idea what it was even when they were getting the money.

insights.claim: Lowrey's proposed fix for invisible benefits is for the IRS to mail physical checks printed with the program name rather than using direct deposit, deliberately trading elegance for political visibility.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: A concrete, low-cost design change that would materially raise the perceived salience — and therefore the survival odds — of any future refundable credit.

insights.claim: Disability insurance is already extraordinarily onerous to obtain: in 5 percent of applications the applicant submits more than 1,000 pages of medical paperwork, and 11,000 Americans die each year waiting on a disability determination.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: The mortality-while-waiting figure is the strongest available rebuttal to the standard fiscal proposal of tightening disability screening further.
insights.quote: 11,000 Americans die waiting on a disability determination each year.

insights.claim: Lowrey attributes the roughly fourfold rise in disability insurance enrollment from 1990 to 2014 to population aging and rising chronic conditions tied to obesity rather than to fraud, and notes the caseload has fallen substantially since 2014.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: If DI growth was demographic and health-driven rather than fraud-driven, the post-2014 decline is a labor-market signal rather than evidence that enforcement worked.

insights.claim: Lowrey argues fraud in Medicare and Medicaid is almost entirely on the provider side — nursing homes, doctors' offices and hospital systems — because large-scale fraud requires high claim-processing volume that no individual beneficiary can generate.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Enforcement aimed at beneficiaries is misallocated; a genuine crackdown would land on provider revenue, which is the real exposure for nursing-home and post-acute operators.
insights.quote: the problem with fraud is almost all on the provider side

insights.claim: Lowrey holds that more administrative burden would not have prevented pandemic-era fraud, which was driven largely by criminal organizations setting up sham small businesses and exploiting unprepared unemployment insurance systems.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the common post-2020 inference that loosened verification caused the fraud wave — her causal claim is capability failure, not leniency.
insights.quote: I do not think that time taxes, administrative burdens, having more of them, would have prevented the fraud at all.

insights.claim: State unemployment insurance systems remain on ancient infrastructure — literally running COBOL — because a governor facing low unemployment has no political incentive to fund upgrades to a system that only matters in recessions.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: A structural, recurring failure mode: expect the same UI breakdown and fraud surge in the next recession, with emergency IT procurement spiking then rather than now.
insights.quote: If you’re a governor and you have a low unemployment rate, what governor is going to devote a huge amount of money to upgrading a state UI system?

insights.claim: Lowrey separates improper payments from purposeful fraud, arguing improper payment rates are a direct function of rule complexity — demanding monthly gross and net income over six months from people who do not own a computer guarantees errors — so simplification would cut both error rates and bureaucratic cost.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Reframes headline improper-payment statistics as a measure of program design failure rather than citizen dishonesty, which changes what a credible integrity reform looks like.
insights.quote: Improper payments are a function of the complexity of this system.

insights.claim: Lowrey supports easier front-end access paired with back-end auditing but rejects adding obscenely harsh randomized punishments, arguing reasonable audits and the threat of civil penalties suffice and that fraud requires proving intent.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Marks the live design choice in any benefits modernization — front-end verification versus back-end audit — with very different vendor and compliance implications.
insights.quote: Why do you need the harsh punishment as opposed to the auditing and the threat of that and the threat of civil penalties?

insights.claim: Lowrey argues fraud narratives function politically to make programs seem illegitimate so voters will tolerate cuts they would not otherwise support, even though she considers the benefit fraud rate quite low.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Fraud headlines are a leading indicator of program-cut legislation regardless of the dollar amounts involved — watch the narrative rather than the audit figures.
insights.quote: fraud has also been a way of making these programs seem illegitimate so that voters will tolerate cutting them

insights.claim: Cowen contends the Minnesota Medicaid fraud involving Somali autism claims probably involved little money but became an outsized headline that degraded both policy and discourse, and argues tighter individual procedures would have protected system integrity.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Shows how small-dollar, high-salience fraud events drive disproportionate policy and immigration-politics shifts — a tail risk for both programs and immigration-sensitive sectors.

insights.claim: Cowen argues explicitly for using time taxes as a rationing device — forcing patients through hoops for knee and back surgeries that often do not work — on the grounds that most ways of saving money are not nice.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Names an underdiscussed Medicare cost-control lever that would hit elective orthopedic volumes; expanded prior authorization is its real-world implementation.
insights.quote: Shouldn’t we just be tougher and force people to go through more hoops? I know it’s not nice, but most ways of saving money are not nice.

insights.claim: Lowrey rejects paperwork rationing of medical care as illegitimate and unfair because it allocates treatment to whoever is good at paperwork, preferring lower payment rates that make a procedure unprofitable for doctors to perform.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Price-based rationing hits provider margins while paperwork rationing hits patient volumes — different sectors bear the cost depending on which tool policymakers pick.
insights.quote: It shouldn’t be that if you are going to get your knee repaired, it’s because you have Medicare and are good at paperwork.

insights.claim: Lowrey identifies government price controls on pharmaceuticals as the single most popular policy proposal among both Democrats and Republicans and the highest-leverage way to reduce medical spending.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Bipartisan popularity means drug price controls carry political risk independent of which party wins — a persistent overhang on pharma pricing power.
insights.quote: There’s no more popular policy proposal out there for both Democrats and Republicans than having the government do price controls in more pharmaceuticals.

insights.claim: Lowrey argues the most psychologically torturous burdens are deliberately invasive questions on assistance applications — height and weight, the paternity of children, where and on what day they were conceived — which signal that the government wants the process to be painful.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Explains take-up shortfalls that income-eligibility models miss: the deterrent is dignity cost, not time cost, and automation cannot remove it.
insights.quote: That’s the stuff that I think it’s the government saying that it doesn’t care about you. That it wants it to be painful.

insights.claim: Cowen argues that making benefits outright impossible to obtain is not technically a time tax — because people who know they cannot qualify never apply — yet achieves the same deterrent effect at lower overhead, a distinction Lowrey concedes in form but rejects in practice.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Clean eligibility bars deliver the same fiscal savings as deterrence-by-friction without the administrative cost — an argument for rule clarity over process complexity.
insights.quote: If you know you can’t get it, you don’t bother to apply, but it’s like a time tax in the sense that it keeps you away from the benefit.

insights.claim: Cowen argues voting should not be made too easy because lower participation costs skew turnout toward less educated voters who on average make worse choices, while Lowrey refuses outcome-based arguments entirely and says voting should be as easy as possible on pure principle.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Crystallizes the deepest disagreement of the conversation — whether administrative friction is ever a legitimate quality filter — with voting as the hardest test case.
insights.quote: I think my view is only principled. I don’t care about outcomes.

insights.claim: Lowrey attributes the better administrative performance of small countries to federalism and ethnic homogeneity — citing Finland as basically ethnically Finnish — producing higher social trust that the racially and ethnically diverse United States cannot replicate.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: If homogeneity rather than policy design drives Nordic administrative quality, importing Nordic program design into the US without federal consolidation will underdeliver.
insights.quote: I think it’s homogeneity.

insights.claim: Lowrey wants mass programs administered federally wherever legally possible, pointing to more than 100 separate TANF programs and 56 Medicaid programs as pure overhead multiplication in a country where people move between states constantly.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Quantifies fragmentation cost in US safety-net administration and identifies consolidation as the largest available efficiency gain — and the largest disruption to state-level program vendors.
insights.quote: We have more than 100 TANF programs. We have 56 Medicaid programs.

insights.claim: Lowrey argues federal programs are generally better managed than state ones partly because the federal government has no balanced budget rule and spends more than it takes in tax revenue every year.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: State balanced-budget constraints are the structural reason state service delivery degrades precisely when demand spikes in a downturn — a procyclical failure worth pricing into recession scenarios.

insights.claim: Lowrey argues government ineffectiveness is itself a major driver of collapsing public confidence, citing San Francisco where state and city incompetence at building and housing policy produced a pox-on-everybody's-house attitude.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Links administrative failure directly to anti-incumbent political volatility — the channel by which local delivery failures become national political risk.
insights.quote: we have a huge problem with trust because the government is so ineffective and treats the time of citizens as valueless

insights.claim: Cowen argues the US should zero out its postal service over roughly ten years, citing Denmark abolishing its postal service this year, while Lowrey resists on the grounds that a high-inequality country still has many people without smartphones or computers.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Denmark's abolition is a live precedent that makes a USPS wind-down a more credible medium-term scenario than it looked a few years ago, with implications for last-mile logistics competitors.
insights.quote: Denmark, just this year, abolished its postal service. They don’t have any.

insights.claim: Lowrey observes that essentially all US policy is designed to let people stay in place and that Americans no longer move the way they used to, making any policy of deliberately depopulating rural areas politically impossible.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Place-based subsidy persistence is structural rather than cyclical — rural service and infrastructure spending has a strong political floor regardless of efficiency arguments.
insights.quote: All of our policies are aimed at allowing people to be in place. We’re very stuck as people.

themes.theme: AI Agents and the UBI Case

insights.claim: Cowen predicts that within five years AI agents will handle almost all benefits paperwork for citizens, and Lowrey accepts the timeline while flagging that the lower-income users of the most burdensome programs may not know about or feel comfortable using such agents.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A five-year horizon for agentic form-filling implies the adoption gap, not the capability gap, decides whether AI narrows or widens benefit take-up inequality.
insights.quote: You just say to your agent, “Hey, fill out these benefits form,” and then you go away, you go to sleep and it’s done? Won’t that happen within five years?

insights.claim: Lowrey argues AI agents cannot eliminate much of the burden because a large share of it is not paperwork at all — mandatory interviews, urine screens, and data that is genuinely hard to collect.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Caps the realistic efficiency gain from govtech AI: in-person verification requirements are the binding constraint, and removing them takes statute, not software.
insights.quote: a lot of it is not really paperwork. It’s mandatory interviews, it’s urine screens, it’s collecting data that might be hard to collect

insights.claim: Lowrey identifies the unstable definition of a household as a core obstacle to automating SNAP, since applicants must report how they split the cost of staples with others and the government has no consistent household definition.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: A concrete illustration that benefits automation is a data-definition problem before it is an AI problem — relevant to anyone underwriting govtech implementation timelines.

insights.claim: Lowrey reports she was skeptical of AI's value in benefits administration but was persuaded by the best civic technologist she knows, and sees AI as unusually good at translating legalistic government questions into what is actually being asked.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Translation of legalese, rather than end-to-end automation, is the near-term killer application for AI in public services — a lower-regulatory-risk entry point for vendors.
insights.quote: the best civic technologist I know thinks that it’ll help a lot

insights.claim: Lowrey says post-publication UBI studies have been sobering and she has updated her priors, conceding the ancillary benefits she expected from cash transfers have not materialized, while maintaining the case for cash simply as cash.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: A pro-UBI author publicly downgrading her own evidence base is a meaningful signal that the empirical case for cash-transfer spillovers has weakened.
insights.quote: the studies have been sobering, and, yes, I have updated my priors

insights.claim: Lowrey specifies the macro signature that would force a UBI conversation: GDP and productivity rising radically while unemployment also rises — a combination she calls very strange.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Gives a falsifiable macro tripwire for AI-driven labor displacement: rising productivity alongside rising unemployment is the signal that major redistribution policy becomes live.
insights.quote: if we see a situation in which GDP is radically increasing, productivity is increasing, and unemployment is going up, that would be very strange, and I think we would have to start looking at UBI-type functions

insights.claim: Lowrey says she was extremely dismissive that AI would necessitate UBI when she wrote her earlier book, having regarded Bay Area AI believers in 2018 as religious zealots, and now considers herself to have been very wrong after using ChatGPT.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: A documented belief reversal by a previously skeptical mainstream economics journalist marks how far elite consensus on AI capability has shifted since 2018.
insights.quote: I was extremely dismissive at the time of the notion that AIs would necessitate UBI.

insights.claim: Cowen proposes that UBI's purpose under an AI boom is not to raise happiness but to stop people becoming less happy due to instability, making system stability rather than welfare gain the benchmark — a framing Lowrey endorses.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Reframes UBI as political-stability insurance for an AI transition rather than an anti-poverty program, changing both the cost-benefit test and the likely coalition behind it.

insights.claim: Lowrey argues businesses systematically minimize time taxes for customers who are spending and maximize them — as far as legally allowed — for customers trying to stop spending, with the health system the worst bureaucratic morass in the private sector.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Asymmetric friction is a measurable driver of retention revenue, so click-to-cancel style regulation is a direct margin risk for subscription and insurance businesses.
insights.quote: businesses have every incentive to reduce time taxes for people who are consuming things and to increase them as much as they are legally allowed to

insights.claim: Lowrey notes reimbursement friction creates a threshold below which people simply forgo money they are owed because they value their time and blood pressure more, and that airlines have replaced cash bounce-off compensation rules with miles and credits.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: Breakage from friction is a real revenue line for airlines and expense systems, and her prescription — give people cash — is the regulatory direction that would erase it.
insights.quote: There’s some amount that you just won’t do it because you value your own time and your blood pressure, right?

insights.claim: Lowrey argues white-collar labor-saving technology is Jevons-paradoxical: anything designed like email to make life easier eventually makes it worse by multiplying the number of tasks and the things companies can do to you, citing passkeys and password managers.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to the assumption that AI productivity gains show up as reclaimed time rather than expanded task volume — relevant to any thesis pricing in white-collar headcount cuts.
insights.quote: I’m convinced it’s all Jevons paradoxical.

insights.claim: Cowen argues a harsh, stingy US benefits system acts as a positive selection filter attracting more ambitious and self-sustaining immigrants, which matters enormously given low native fertility.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Frames benefit stinginess as immigration policy by other means — a rationale for restricting safety-net access that is independent of fiscal cost.
insights.quote: If we have a welfare system where it’s really hard to get benefits, don’t we, in fact, attract a higher quality of immigrant, more ambitious people and more self-sustaining, than if benefits are just easy to get?

insights.claim: Lowrey counters that the welfare magnet hypothesis did not pan out empirically, that immigrants are already barred from much of the safety net for long periods, and that direct policies such as an automatic Green Card for anyone earning a US PhD would attract talent far more effectively than indirect deterrence.
insights.speaker: Annie Lowrey
insights.so_what: If the welfare magnet effect is empirically weak, benefit restrictions buy no selection benefit and visa design is the only lever that actually moves talent flows.
insights.quote: My understanding was that the welfare magnet hypothesis didn’t pan out.

insights.claim: Cowen rejects the automatic-Green-Card-for-PhDs proposal on the grounds that most PhDs are lazy and the credential has become negatively selected relative to IQ, preferring more O-1 visas and H-1B reform without $100,000 fees.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A pointed claim that academic credentials are a deteriorating proxy for talent, favoring achievement-based visa categories over degree-based ones in any immigration reform.
insights.quote: I know plenty of lazy PhDs. Most PhDs are lazy, I would say.
